conversation.content: Let's design a persistent key-value store — something like a simplified Redis that survives restarts. What questions do you have?
So we're building something like Redis? What kind of operations do we need to support?

Basic GET, PUT, and DELETE. Keys are strings, values are binary blobs up to 10KB. We need to handle 50K writes/sec and 200K reads/sec with 5TB of data. The key requirement is durability — data must survive server restarts. Let's start with a single-node design.
Okay. So for GET and PUT, the simplest approach is a hash map in memory. Keys map to values. GET is O(1), PUT is O(1). Fast and simple.
What happens when the server restarts? You have 5TB of data in a hash map in memory.
Oh... we lose everything? Because it's all in RAM. That's the problem. We need to write to disk somehow.
Right. So how would you add persistence? When a PUT comes in, what do you do to ensure the data survives a crash?
We could write every PUT to a file on disk. Like, append the key and value to a log file. Then on startup, we replay the log to rebuild the hash map.

Good instinct — you've essentially described a Write-Ahead Log, or WAL. This is how most databases ensure durability. But there's a problem: 5TB of data won't fit in memory for your hash map. What do you do?
Oh right, 5TB is way too much for RAM. Hmm. So we can't keep everything in the hash map. We need some data on disk. Maybe we write to disk and only keep frequently accessed data in memory as a cache?
Right. But how do you organize the data on disk so that reads are efficient? If everything is just appended to a log, finding a specific key means scanning the entire file.

We could keep an index in memory that maps each key to its position in the file. So on a GET, we look up the offset in the index and seek directly to that position on disk. The index itself is small — just keys and file offsets — so it could fit in memory even if the values don't.
That's actually close to how Bitcask works — a real storage engine. What's the problem with an append-only log when you update the same key multiple times? Say key 'foo' is PUT 1000 times.

The file keeps growing because we have 1000 entries for 'foo' but only the last one matters. The old ones are wasted space. We'd need to clean that up somehow... like go through the file and remove old entries?
That process is called compaction. You'd write a new file with only the latest version of each key. But you can't modify the active log while it's being written to. How would you handle that?

Maybe we use multiple files? Like, when the current log file reaches a certain size, we close it and start a new one. The old files can be compacted in the background while new writes go to the active file.

Good. Now at 50K writes/sec, your write path is: append to WAL, update in-memory index. That's fast. But the read path — you said you look up the file offset and do a disk seek. At 200K reads/sec, how many disk seeks can a single SSD handle?
I'm not sure... maybe 50,000? 100,000? I know SSDs are faster than HDDs for random reads but I don't know the exact numbers.
A good NVMe SSD can do about 500K random reads per second, so one SSD could theoretically handle it. But in practice you need caching. What would you cache?

The most frequently accessed key-value pairs. Like an LRU cache in memory. If the key is in the cache, return it directly without hitting disk. If not, read from disk and add it to the cache. For the cache size, if we have 64GB of RAM and the index takes maybe 10GB, we have 54GB left for caching values. That's a decent amount.
Now what about distributing this across multiple nodes for scalability? How would you shard 5TB across machines?
We could hash each key and use modulo to assign it to a node. Like if we have 10 nodes, hash(key) mod 10 tells us which node owns that key.
What happens when you need to add an 11th node? With modulo sharding, almost every key remaps to a different node.
Oh, that's bad. Basically all the data would need to be reshuffled. There's something called consistent hashing that fixes this, right? Where adding a node only moves a fraction of the keys?
Yes, consistent hashing is the standard solution. What about replication? If a node goes down, its data is lost.

We'd replicate each key to multiple nodes. Maybe 3 copies. If one node goes down, the data is still available on the other two. We'd need to keep the replicas in sync... maybe write to all three on every PUT?
Writing to all three synchronously means your write latency is determined by the slowest replica. What's a common alternative?
Write to 2 out of 3 and consider it successful? Then the third one catches up asynchronously. I think that's called a quorum write.
Right — W + R > N gives you consistency. We're out of time. Any final thoughts?

I think the design is a WAL for durability, an in-memory index for fast lookups, segmented log files with background compaction, and consistent hashing with quorum replication for distribution. I learned a lot during this discussion — I didn't realize how much goes into making a KV store durable and distributed.
You arrived at the right building blocks with guidance. The instinct for append-only logging was good. Thanks for working through it.

strengths: Good instinct for append-only log — arrived at WAL concept independently
In-memory index for file offsets was a solid insight
Able to build on interviewer's hints and make progress
weaknesses: Started with 'hash map in memory' for 5TB of data — didn't consider durability or memory limits
No knowledge of storage engine fundamentals — LSM trees, B-trees, SSTables not mentioned
Couldn't estimate SSD performance — crucial for a storage system design
Consistent hashing and quorum replication were only mentioned after heavy hinting
No discussion of failure detection, data repair, or operational concerns
